nameStory: Crimson clover gets its vivid name from its spectacular bright red flower heads that look like they've been dipped in rich crimson paint. The word 'clover' comes from the Old English 'clæfre,' referring to the plant's distinctive three-leaflet pattern that has symbolized good luck for centuries.
description: Crimson clover is an annual flowering plant that grows 1-3 feet tall with soft, fuzzy stems and the classic three-part clover leaves. Its most striking feature is the brilliant red, cone-shaped flower head that sits atop each stem like a fuzzy crimson torch. Originally from Europe and southwest Asia, this eye-catching plant has made itself at home in fields, roadsides, and gardens across New England. Unlike many of its clover cousins, crimson clover grows as an annual, completing its entire life cycle in one growing season.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Brilliant crimson-red flower heads shaped like elongated cones or torpedoes, about 1-2 inches long, made up of dozens of tiny tubular flowers packed tightly together with a soft, fuzzy texture

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Classic three-leaflet clover pattern with oval leaflets that feel soft and slightly fuzzy, often with subtle lighter green markings or spots on the surface

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright annual plant growing 1-3 feet tall with multiple branching stems that feel soft and hairy to the touch, forming loose clusters rather than dense mats

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Distinctly fuzzy, soft stems covered in fine white hairs that give them a velvety texture when you run your fingers along them

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Small, hard, yellowish seeds develop within the dried flower heads, which turn brown and papery as they mature in late summer

habitat: Look for crimson clover in disturbed soils like roadsides, field edges, abandoned lots, and agricultural areas throughout New England. It thrives in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soils and prefers full sun to partial shade. Often found mixed with other weedy plants and grasses in areas that have been recently disturbed or cultivated.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge with their characteristic three-part leaves, growing rapidly in cool spring weather as rosettes before sending up flowering stems.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season when the spectacular crimson flower heads are most visible and vibrant, attracting bees and other pollinators from June through August.
seasonality.fall: Flower heads turn brown and dry, releasing seeds, while the entire plant begins to die back as this annual completes its life cycle.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground presence as an annual plant, but seeds lie dormant in the soil waiting for spring germination.

funFact: Crimson clover was so prized by early American farmers that it was called 'German clover' and 'Italian clover' depending on which European seed stock they imported - and a single flower head contains enough individual tiny flowers to potentially produce over 100 seeds!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with red clover, but crimson clover's flower heads are distinctly cone-shaped and bright crimson rather than red clover's rounded, pinkish-purple globes. Memory trick: 'Crimson cones' versus 'red rounds' - the shapes match the colors!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'crimson clover,' this plant is actually a relatively recent arrival to New England, introduced from Europe as a forage crop. Many people assume all clovers are native wildflowers, but crimson clover is actually an agricultural escape that has naturalized in the wild.
compareHints: Crimson clover stands out from other New England clovers by its distinctive torpedo-shaped, brilliant red flower heads - no other local clover has this intense crimson color or elongated cone shape. Red clover has rounded purple-pink heads, white clover has white globe-shaped flowers, and the hop clovers have tiny yellow flower clusters that look completely different.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's clovers, red clover is the tallest and most upright, while white clover creeps along the ground and has white flowers.
Among New England clovers, white clover is unique for its creeping growth habit and pure white spherical flowers.

Among New England clovers, rabbitfoot clover is unique for its fuzzy, pale, cylindrical flower heads - completely different from the round pink heads of red clover, the round white heads of white clover, or the small yellow clusters of hop clovers.
Among New England's yellow-flowered clovers, large hop clover stands tallest and most erect, while hop trefoil sprawls closer to the ground with smaller flowers.

Among New England's yellow-flowered clovers, hop trefoil stands out with its distinctive oval, hop-shaped flower heads compared to the round heads of large hop clover or the tiny heads of lesser hop trefoil.
Among New England's clovers, alsike is the tall one with color-changing flowers.
Among New England's clovers, lesser hop trefoil stands out for its tiny size and bright yellow flowers - most other clovers have white, pink, or red blooms.
Zigzag clover differs from red clover by having narrower leaflets without white markings and distinctive angled stems.
